# Episode 1 — script (generated from script.tpl.md and out/claims.json; do not edit)


## cold-open

- `co-bars` A lower rate cuts the monthly payment.
- `co-bill` But the refinance has a price, and the savings must repay it first.
- `co-question` So how far do rates have to fall before a refinance pays for itself?

## act1

- `a1-lab` This is a lab for money decisions: we run the numbers on public data and show every assumption.
- `a1-scope` US only. The rates here are history, not a forecast.
- `a1-rehook` By the end, you will see the exact rate drop that repays a typical refinance within 36 months, and how every rate drop since 1971 actually played out.
- `a1-rates` Here is the rate itself: the weekly average for a 30-year fixed mortgage, from Freddie Mac's survey.
- `a1-peak` It peaked at 18.63% in 1981.
- `a1-low` It bottomed at 2.65% in 2021.
- `a1-drops` Every fall in that line is a moment when homeowners asked the same question.
- `a1-q` First question, then: what does a refinance actually cost?
- `a1-hmda` Lenders report it for every loan they make, under the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act, as total loan costs.
- `a1-terms` Those are the closing costs: origination charges, discount points, the appraisal, title insurance, and the rest.
- `a1-points` Discount points are optional: paying more at closing buys a lower rate, so part of that bill is a choice.
- `a1-cashout` Cash-out refinances, which also take equity out of the house, cost more: a median of $8,655. This film keeps to refinances that change only the rate and the term.
- `a1-count` In 2025, lenders reported 488,241 of those, into 30-year first mortgages.
- `a1-median` In nominal dollars, the median one cost $5,124.
- `a1-spread` The middle half paid between $3,443 and $8,270.
- `a1-boom` The count follows the rate. In 2021, near the bottom, lenders reported 3,089,298 of them.
- `a1-boomcost` Their median bill that year was $3,406.
- `a1-turn` But the dollar figure hides the real pattern. The bill barely grows with the size of the loan.
- `a1-small` On loans under $150,000, the median cost was 3.4% of the amount borrowed.
- `a1-big` On loans of $750,000 and more, it was 0.5%.
- `a1-keep` So the same cut in rate repays a large loan faster than a small one. Keep that in mind; it comes back.
- `a1-rule` Paying the bill back is simple division: the closing costs, divided by the drop in the monthly payment.
- `a1-payoff` The answer is the break-even: the month when the savings have covered the bill.
- `a1-after` Before that month, the refinance is still in the red. After it, every payment is money kept.

## act2

- `a2-q` Now the main question: how big does the drop have to be?
- `a2-loan` Take the median refinance: a balance of $375,000, and $5,124 to close.
- `a2-old` Say the old loan carries 7.62%, the average rate in the month the last big drop began, October 2023.
- `a2-s025` Cut the rate by 0.25 points, and the payment falls by $64 a month.
- `a2-be025` At that pace, the bill takes 80 months to come back.
- `a2-s05` Double the cut to 0.5 points, and the payment falls by $128 a month.
- `a2-be05` Break-even arrives in 41 months.
- `a2-s10` A cut of 1 point saves $253 a month.
- `a2-be10` That pays back the bill in 21 months.
- `a2-s20` 2 points pay back in 11 months, well inside a year.
- `a2-curve` Look at the shape of that curve. It is not a straight line.
- `a2-cliff` Below 0.5 points it climbs steeply: each smaller cut adds years, not months.
- `a2-thumb` That is where the common rule of thumb about a full point comes from: for this loan, 1 point pays back in 21 months, 0.5 points in 41.
- `a2-turn` But remember the pattern in the costs, and move the same question to a different loan.
- `a2-mid` To break even within 36 months, the median loan needs a cut of 0.56 points.
- `a2-small` A loan under $150,000 needs 1.32 points, because its bill is a bigger share of the balance.
- `a2-big` A loan of $750,000 or more needs only 0.2.
- `a2-hold60` Give the median loan 60 months instead, and 0.33 points is enough.
- `a2-hold84` Give it 84 months, and it needs 0.24.
- `a2-flip` Read each of those as a flip point: below it, the bill outlasts the stay; above it, the savings win.
- `a2-payoff` So there is no single threshold. The drop that pays back depends on two things: how big the loan is, and how long it is kept.
- `a2-hold` And how long it is kept is the one number no dataset can supply.
- `a2-reset` One more cost hides inside the new loan. It starts a fresh 30 years, so the last payment moves further away, even when each payment is smaller.
- `a2-reset2` The simple division ignores that. It answers only the first question: when do the savings cover the bill?

## act3

- `a3-q` The division assumes the new rate is the last one. What happened in the real drops?
- `a3-all` We found every fall of at least 1 point in the 30-year rate since 1971: 13 of them.
- `a3-rules` In each, a borrower who took a loan at the peak refinances in the first month the rate is 1 point lower.
- `a3-costs` Closing costs use the median share for that year; before 2018, lenders did not report them, so a fixed share is used and marked illustrative.
- `a3-80s` The steepest falls came in the early 1980s.
- `a3-81` After the peak of 1981, the first cut of 1 point came 2 months later.
- `a3-81be` It paid back in 13 months, but the slide went on, and the next point came 9 months after the refinance.
- `a3-short` Some drops were brief. The fall that began in 1987 lasted 4 months, and the refinance came at its very bottom.
- `a3-06` The drop that began in 2006 was slower. The refinance came in January 2008, and it had paid for itself before the next point arrived.
- `a3-range` At a cut of 1 point, break-even took between 10 and 21 months across all 13 drops.
- `a3-turn` But in 5 of them, the rate kept falling: another drop of 1 point before the first refinance had paid for itself.
- `a3-twice` Those borrowers met the same question twice, and a second refinance starts a new clock with a new bill.
- `a3-example` In the drop that began in November 2018, the refinance came in June 2019.
- `a3-example2` It needed 18 months to break even, and the next drop of 1 point came only 17 months later.
- `a3-quiet` In the other 8, the first refinance was the one that mattered.
- `a3-23` The latest drop began in October 2023. The cut of 1 point arrived in August 2024.
- `a3-23be` At that year's median cost, it paid back in 21 months.
- `a3-answer` So, how far do rates have to fall before a refinance pays for itself?
- `a3-answer2` For the median loan and median costs, a cut that repays it within 36 months is 0.56 points.
- `a3-answer3` Half as much patience asks for more: to pay back in 21 months takes 1 point.
- `a3-limit` That answer has limits. It counts payment savings only: no taxes, no return on the cash, and a new 30-year loan restarts the clock on owning the house outright.
- `a3-median` It uses medians: half of borrowers paid more than $5,124, and an offered rate can differ from the survey average.
- `a3-history` And it is history, not a forecast: nothing here says where rates go next.
- `a3-close` What history does show is the shape of the trade: a known bill up front, against savings that arrive one month at a time, for as long as the loan lasts.

## method

- `m-rates` Method. Rates are Freddie Mac's weekly survey via FRED, checked against the Optimal Blue index since 2017.
- `m-drops` A drop counts when the monthly average falls at least 1 point from a peak before rising 1 point from its low.
- `m-costs` Costs are HMDA loan-level data from 2018 to 2025: originated refinances, first lien, 30-year term.
- `m-assume` Closing costs are paid in cash, with no taxes and no discounting. Every figure and formula is listed in the description.

## outro

- `o-recap` A small cut needs a long stay. A large loan needs a smaller cut. And a falling rate can make the first refinance too early.
- `o-close` The break-even is simple division. The hard part is the number only the borrower knows: how long the loan will be kept.
- `o-bill` The bill is known the day the loan closes. The savings arrive one month at a time.
- `o-sources` The sources are linked in the description, and the next decision is already on the bench.
